The source prints the tenderness site as the pericardial area; it is kept as written and not reinterpreted as another site.

The source says the diverticulitis was treated with antibiotics (abstract and case text) and that cefmetazole was started, but does not say whether the generic antibiotics and cefmetazole are the same course, so they are kept as two items. No dose, route or duration is stated for either.
The statement that the stone could have been identified by the high CT value on the first enhanced CT is a retrospective comment and is not recorded as a first-CT finding.

Discussion statements about published cases, general epidemiology, the possibility of recurrence and the first-report claim are not patient facts. The statement that the patient survived because the fistula formed in the intestinal tract is an authors' explanation and is not recorded as a fact.

The text gives the endoscopic procedure on day 9 and discharge on the 17th day without naming what the days count from, so the two day numbers are not used as same-anchor times; the procedure-to-discharge order rests on the abstract (the successful treatment made her discharged) and on in-hospital care preceding the discharge of the same stay. No calendar dates are stated.

The discussion sentence "Herein, CT images revealed no stones in the bile duct or gallbladder" is taken as describing this single case; it does not say which CT (admission contrast-enhanced or repeat plain CT), so the refuted stones are not linked to a CT event.

The admission temperature is 35.8°C, yet after cefmetazole the text says the patient continued to have a fever; no febrile temperature is printed and the two statements refer to different times, so both are kept as written.

The abstract says the disease was treated with antibiotics and not cured; the case text names generic antibiotics at admission and later cefmetazole. The non-cure outcome is ordered after the generic antibiotic start and before the endoscopic removal, and is not attached to the cefmetazole item.
